content.title: About
content.content: Meatball soup is a classic Russian dish consisting of a flavorful broth with small meatballs. Made from beef or pork, onion, carrot, potato and spices, it combines nourishment with a comforting taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the 19th century and quickly became a staple in working‑class families.
Meatballs are usually a mixture of beef and pork, sometimes enriched with rice or semolina for a softer texture.
Traditional recipes include a bay leaf and whole black peppercorns.
The soup is often served with sour cream and fresh herbs.
During the Soviet era it was a common first course in school cafeterias.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Meatballs provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef and pork contain heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The soup supplies vitamins B12 and B6, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Vegetable nutrients
items.content: Potato, carrot and onion add fiber, vitamin C and potassium.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: A warm broth helps maintain fluid balance, especially in cold weather.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Using ready‑made broth cubes can raise salt levels; adjust seasoning accordingly.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rare individuals allergic to beef or pork may experience reactions.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Fat depends on the cut of meat; choose lean cuts or trim excess fat.

items.title: Thorough cooking
items.content: Meatballs must be fully cooked to eliminate the risk of food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, often topped with a dollop of sour cream, fresh dill or parsley, and a slice of rye bread. Meatballs can be gently mashed with a fork for a softer bite.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat until boiling to ensure safety.
